stem: Which of the following risks is insurable under a life insurance contract?

options.A: The risk of losing money at a casino
options.B: The risk of premature death of the life insured
options.C: The risk of not making an expected profit on a business venture
options.D: The risk of loss on a share portfolio bought on the stock exchange

explanation: Only pure risk (loss or no loss) is insurable; premature death is a pure risk. Shares, gambling and expected profit are speculative risks with an upside, so insurance cannot cover them because insurance compensates a loss, it does not hand a profit.

stem: Which characteristic would make a risk UNINSURABLE by a private insurer?

options.A: The loss occurs by chance and is not deliberate
options.B: A single event could be catastrophic and bankrupt the insurer
options.C: A large number of similar exposure units exists
options.D: The loss is definite and can be measured

explanation: A catastrophic exposure that could bankrupt the insurer (e.g. a nuclear event) fails the requirements for an insurable risk. The other three options are all requirements that an insurable risk must satisfy.

stem: Insurance is best described as which method of dealing with risk?

options.A: Risk control
options.B: Risk transfer
options.C: Risk retention
options.D: Risk avoidance

explanation: Insurance is a risk-transfer mechanism: the individual transfers the financial consequence of a pure risk to the insurer. Retention (self-insurance) is the opposite, where you keep the risk yourself.

stem: Which of the following is one of the three personal risks that life insurance is designed to address?

options.A: The risk of outliving one's financial resources
options.B: The risk of a fire destroying one's home
options.C: The risk of a stock market crash
options.D: The risk of a motor accident damaging one's car

explanation: Life insurance addresses premature death, outliving your resources (longevity risk), and poor health or disablement. Fire and motor damage are property risks handled by general insurance, not life insurance.

stem: Ben takes out a policy on the life of his wife Cara, with himself as the person who owns and pays for the policy. In this arrangement, who is the life insured?

options.A: Cara, because it is her life that is covered
options.B: Both Ben and Cara equally
options.C: Whoever is named as the beneficiary
options.D: Ben, because he owns and pays for the policy

explanation: The life insured is the person whose life is covered, here Cara. Ben is the policy owner. Owner and life insured can be different people (a third-party policy), which is a classic exam trap.

stem: The guaranteed lump sum stated on the first page of a life policy that is paid on a valid claim is known as the:

options.A: Sum assured
options.B: Loading
options.C: Surrender value
options.D: Cash value

explanation: The sum assured (face amount or face value) is the guaranteed amount payable on a claim, shown on the first page of the policy. Cash value is the accumulated savings element, not the guaranteed claim amount.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes insurance from gambling?

options.A: Insurance is zero-sum, while gambling is mutually beneficial
options.B: Gambling creates a new speculative risk, whereas insurance transfers an existing pure risk
options.C: Both insurance and gambling create new risk that did not previously exist
options.D: Gambling handles an existing risk while insurance creates a new one

explanation: Gambling manufactures a new speculative risk and is zero-sum; insurance handles an existing pure risk, creates nothing new, and is socially productive. The reverse claim, that insurance creates the new risk, is the common confusion.

stem: An applicant deliberately understates his weight and hides a family history of heart disease on the proposal form. This dishonesty is an example of:

options.A: A peril
options.B: Anti-selection
options.C: Physical hazard
options.D: Moral hazard

explanation: Moral hazard is dishonest behaviour connected to insurance, such as lying on the form. Physical hazard would be the actual obesity or heart condition itself; a peril is the cause of loss, not the behaviour.

stem: What is the insurer's main defence against anti-selection (adverse selection)?

options.A: Charging every applicant the same standard premium
options.B: Offering a free-look period on all policies
options.C: Underwriting to classify applicants as standard, sub-standard or declined
options.D: Paying bonuses only to healthy policy owners

explanation: Anti-selection is the tendency for higher-risk people to seek cover more eagerly; underwriting classifies and prices applicants (standard, sub-standard, declined) to defend the pool. A flat premium for everyone would worsen anti-selection.

stem: The law of large numbers, which is the mathematical foundation of insurance, states that:

options.A: A larger insurer will always be more profitable than a smaller one
options.B: Premiums must always exceed claims by a large margin
options.C: The larger the sum assured, the smaller the premium charged
options.D: As the number of insured lives grows, actual losses track expected losses more closely

explanation: With more insured lives, actual loss experience converges on the expected (predicted) losses, letting insurers price accurately. It is about predictability of losses, not about premium size or guaranteed profit.

stem: Regarding the duty of utmost good faith on a life insurance policy, which statement is correct?

options.A: The proposer must disclose all material facts known or ought to be known, and the duty revives on alteration
options.B: The duty of disclosure revives each year when the life policy is renewed
options.C: The duty applies only to the insurer, not the proposer
options.D: The proposer need only disclose facts the proposal form specifically asks about

explanation: Utmost good faith requires disclosure of all material facts the proposer knows or ought to know, even if unasked, running to inception and reviving on alteration. Unlike general insurance, a life policy is not renewed annually, so the duty does not revive on renewal.

stem: Under section 57 of the Insurance Act, when must insurable interest exist for a life insurance policy?

options.A: At every premium payment date
options.B: At the time of death only
options.C: At inception and at the time of death
options.D: At inception only

explanation: For life insurance the interest must exist at inception but NOT at time of death. General insurance requires interest at inception AND at the time of loss; marine cargo requires it only at the time of loss.

stem: In which of the following relationships would a person NOT automatically have a recognised insurable interest in another's life?

options.A: A parent insuring the life of their child under 18
options.B: A creditor insuring the life of a debtor
options.C: A person insuring the life of their spouse at the time of marriage
options.D: A person insuring the life of a casual acquaintance

explanation: Insurable interest requires that you benefit from the person living and lose if they die. Spouse, child under 18, and creditor-debtor are recognised, but a casual acquaintance provides no such interest.

stem: The principle of indemnity does NOT apply to which of the following?

options.A: A life insurance death claim
options.B: A fire claim on a warehouse
options.C: A hospitalisation and surgical medical claim
options.D: A motor own-damage claim

explanation: Indemnity restores you to your pre-loss position with no profit and applies to general and health insurance. Life and personal accident are benefit policies paying an agreed sum assured, so they are NOT contracts of indemnity.

stem: In Singapore's insurance market, which body is responsible for resolving disputes between policy owners and insurers through mediation and adjudication?

options.A: MAS
options.B: LIA
options.C: SDIC
options.D: FIDReC

explanation: FIDReC handles dispute resolution through filing, mediation, then adjudication. MAS is the regulator, LIA is the market association, and SDIC provides deposit and policy owner protection, not dispute resolution.

stem: Who sets life insurance premiums, and what balancing act do they perform?

options.A: The board of directors, balancing shareholder returns against solvency
options.B: Underwriters, balancing disclosure against speed of issue
options.C: Financial advisers, balancing commission against client affordability
options.D: Actuaries, balancing expected claims and expenses plus profit against staying competitive

explanation: Actuaries set premiums, balancing three things: covering expected claims, covering expenses plus a profit margin, yet remaining competitive with other insurers. Underwriters assess individual risk, they do not set the premium scale.

stem: Which statement about mortality and morbidity in premium setting is correct?

options.D: Morbidity is the main pricing input for life insurance
options.A: Mortality is the probability of death and morbidity is the rate of sickness or injury
options.B: Health insurance pricing considers morbidity only and ignores mortality entirely
options.C: Mortality tables are compiled without using the law of large numbers

explanation: Mortality is the probability of death at each age; morbidity is the rate of sickness and injury and is the main input for health insurance. Health pricing still also considers mortality, so it is wrong to say morbidity is ignored or that mortality plays no part.

stem: How does a higher assumed rate of investment return affect the premium the insurer charges?

options.B: It raises the premium, because more income must be reserved
options.C: It lowers the premium, because expected returns offset part of the cost
options.D: It has no effect, as investment income is not used in pricing
options.A: It lowers the loading but raises the net premium

explanation: Insurers invest the early-year surplus from level premiums and use expected returns to reduce the premium, so a higher assumed interest rate means a lower premium. Investment income is a core pricing input, so the claim that it has no effect is incorrect.

stem: Which formula correctly describes the premium the proposer actually pays?

options.A: Gross premium = net premium + loading
options.B: Net premium = loading minus gross premium
options.C: Loading = gross premium + net premium
options.D: Net premium = gross premium + loading

explanation: Net premium covers protection (mortality/morbidity plus investment income); loading covers expenses plus profit. Gross premium = net + loading, and the gross premium is what the proposer pays.

stem: How does gender typically affect premiums across life and health insurance?

options.A: Female premiums are lower for life but tend to be higher for health insurance
options.B: Gender is not permitted as a rating factor in Singapore
options.C: Female premiums are higher for both life and health insurance
options.D: Female premiums are lower for both life and health insurance

explanation: For life insurance women generally pay less because they live longer (reduction-in-age method); for health insurance women tend to pay more due to higher hospitalisation, especially above 65. The gender effect flips between the two lines.

stem: Why do non-smokers typically receive a discount on life insurance premiums?

options.A: Because smoking status is not verifiable so all applicants get the discount
options.B: Because they always buy larger sum assured amounts
options.C: Because they statistically enjoy better health and longer life expectancy
options.D: Because they are legally entitled to a rebate under the Insurance Act

explanation: Non-smokers receive discounts because they statistically enjoy better health and live longer, lowering the mortality cost. There is no statutory entitlement, and the discount is not tied to the sum assured.

stem: How is a volume discount for a large sum assured normally applied?

options.A: As a flat cash rebate deducted from the total premium
options.B: As a reduction to the per-$1,000 rate charged
options.C: As a waiver of the first year's premium entirely
options.D: As bonus units added to the policy

explanation: Premiums are quoted per $1,000 of sum assured. Because some admin costs are fixed, large policies get a volume discount applied as a reduction to the per-$1,000 rate, not a flat rebate.

stem: Compared with an annual mode, why does a monthly premium mode usually carry a small surcharge?

options.A: Because monthly policies have a larger sum assured
options.B: Because monthly mode attracts higher commission
options.C: Because a single premium is always cheaper than any instalment mode
options.D: Because the insurer loses interest and incurs more processing on frequent instalments

explanation: More frequent modes carry a small surcharge for lost interest and extra processing. A single premium is lower overall because the insurer receives the whole amount upfront to invest, but that describes single premium, not why monthly carries a surcharge.

stem: Which premium types are permitted when a policy is funded with CPF monies?

options.A: Only regular and yearly renewable premiums
options.B: Only limited premium policies
options.C: Any premium type including limited-pay
options.D: Only single or recurrent single premiums

explanation: CPF monies can buy only single or recurrent single premium policies. Regular, yearly renewable and limited-pay modes are not permitted with CPF funding.

stem: Life insurance products can be classified in four ways. Which statement about these classifications is correct?

options.A: They are four independent lenses, and a policy sits in all four at once
options.B: Premium type is not a valid basis of classification
options.C: Only statutory fund and ownership apply to par policies
options.D: They form a strict hierarchy, so a policy sits in only one at a time

explanation: The four bases (statutory fund, product type, premium type, ownership) are independent lenses, not a hierarchy; a single policy sits in all four simultaneously. They are not mutually exclusive tiers.

stem: Under section 17 of the Insurance Act, which statutory fund MUST be kept separate?

options.B: The participating fund
options.C: The non-participating fund
options.D: The investment-linked fund
options.A: All three funds must always be kept separate from each other

explanation: Par and non-par business may share a fund, but the investment-linked fund must be kept separate. Only the investment-linked fund is mandatorily separate, so the claim that all three funds must always be separate is incorrect.

stem: Which statement about participating and non-participating policies is correct?

options.C: Whole Life can only ever be participating
options.D: Term insurance is typically written as a participating policy
options.A: Whole Life and Endowment can be either participating or non-participating
options.B: Non-participating policies always pay bonuses

explanation: Whole Life and Endowment come in both par and non-par forms, so they cannot be pinned to one side. Term and Universal Life are non-par and pay no bonus, and non-participating policies never pay bonuses, so the other statements are wrong.

stem: Which of the following is classified as a health product rather than a core life product type?

options.A: Disability Income
options.B: Annuity
options.C: Endowment
options.D: Whole Life

explanation: Disability Income is a health product, alongside Critical Illness, Medical Expenses, and Long-Term Care. Endowment, Whole Life and Annuity are core life product types.

stem: Which ownership classification describes the most common arrangement where the policy owner and the life insured are the same person?

options.A: Third-party
options.B: Joint life
options.C: Single life
options.D: Group

explanation: A single life policy has the owner and insured as the same person and is the most common form. Third-party is where owner and insured differ; group covers many lives such as an employer's staff.

stem: A couple takes out a joint life first-to-die policy on their mortgage. When does the benefit pay out and what happens to the cover?

options.A: It pays when both have died, and cover continues for the estate
options.B: It pays on the first death, goes to the survivor, and the cover then ends
options.C: It pays on the first death and continues covering the survivor
options.D: It pays half on each death

explanation: First-to-die pays on the first death, the benefit goes to the survivor and the cover then ends, suiting a joint mortgage. Paying only when both have died describes last survivor (second-to-die), not first-to-die.

stem: Which is an essential characteristic of a group life insurance scheme?

options.A: The group must exist for a purpose other than buying insurance
options.B: The master contract is renewed only once every ten years
options.C: The group may be formed specifically to obtain insurance
options.D: Each member is individually and fully underwritten

explanation: The group must exist for a purpose other than buying insurance; you cannot gather strangers just to obtain group cover. Group schemes use minimal underwriting (a free cover limit) and are renewed yearly, so the claims of individual full underwriting or ten-yearly renewal are wrong.

stem: Group term life insurance is conceptually like a Yearly Renewable Term, but its premium varies according to:

options.A: A fixed rate that never changes
options.B: The stock market performance of the insurer's fund
options.C: The group's size and claims experience
options.D: Each individual member's advancing age

explanation: Group term life premiums vary with the group's size and claims experience, not with each individual member's advancing age. It is the most sold group class in Singapore, usually to age 65 with death and TPD benefits.

stem: Which statement about term insurance is correct?

options.A: It builds cash value that can support a policy loan
options.B: It carries the highest premium of the traditional products
options.C: It pays out on survival to the end of the term
options.D: It pays the sum assured only if the insured dies during the term, and has no cash value

explanation: Term insurance pays only on death during the term, is non-par, has no cash value and carries the lowest premium. Survive the term and you get nothing; no cash value means no policy loan, APL or non-forfeiture options.

stem: A mortgage protection plan whose benefit falls over time to match a reducing loan is an example of which type of term insurance?

options.A: Renewable term
options.B: Decreasing term
options.C: Level term
options.D: Increasing term

explanation: Decreasing term has a falling benefit, matching a reducing mortgage balance. Level term keeps benefit and premium constant (e.g. key-person cover); increasing term rises to counter inflation.

stem: Under a mortgage decreasing term policy, how is each year's sum assured determined?

options.B: It is recalculated each year to equal the exact outstanding loan balance
options.C: It is fixed at outset using assumed rates and repayments, so it may not equal the actual loan
options.D: It rises each year with the interest owed
options.A: It is set by the bank at the time of each claim

explanation: The declining sum assured is fixed at outset using assumed rates and repayments, so the payout may be more or less than the actual outstanding loan. It is not recalculated each year to the real balance, which is the trap.

stem: Why does the premium rise when a renewable term policy is renewed at term-end?

options.A: Because fresh medical evidence lowers the risk classification
options.B: Because the premium rises to the attained age and is pushed up by anti-selection
options.C: Because the insurer adds a cash value component
options.D: Because the sum assured automatically increases on renewal

explanation: Renewal is at attained age without evidence of insurability, and anti-selection pushes the premium up because healthier lives tend to lapse. Yearly renewable term suits the young; do not advise older clients into it.

stem: The convertible option on a term policy gives the owner the right to:

options.A: Surrender the term policy for its cash value
options.B: Increase the sum assured each year without limit
options.C: Renew the term at the original age premium indefinitely
options.D: Convert the term policy into a permanent policy without evidence of insurability

explanation: The convertible option lets the owner convert term into a permanent policy without fresh evidence of insurability. Attained-age conversion is priced at the conversion age (common); original-age conversion is priced at the original age but needs a lump sum and is time-limited.

stem: In the term 'Whole Life insurance', the word 'whole life' refers to:

options.A: The length of the premium-paying period
options.B: The requirement to pay premiums for exactly 100 years
options.C: The fact that no bonuses are ever paid
options.D: The duration of the protection provided

explanation: 'Whole life' refers to the duration of protection (lifetime cover), not how long you pay. Ordinary Whole Life is paid for life while Limited Payment Whole Life is paid over a set period, so the premium term varies.

stem: Why does whole life insurance build cash value while term insurance does not?

options.A: Because term insurers deliberately withhold the savings element
options.B: Because whole life charges level premiums for an event (death) that is certain to occur eventually
options.C: Because term policies invest in riskier assets
options.D: Because cash value is only a marketing feature with no basis

explanation: Cash value arises from charging level premiums for a certain event, since death is guaranteed eventually. Term covers an uncertain event over a limited term, so it accumulates no cash value.

stem: If a whole life policy owner stops paying premiums and makes no election, which non-forfeiture option applies automatically?

options.A: Reduced paid-up insurance
options.B: Automatic Premium Loan
options.C: Surrender for net cash value
options.D: Extended Term Insurance (ETI)

explanation: Extended Term Insurance is the automatic default non-forfeiture option if nothing is elected. Surrender and reduced paid-up must be actively chosen; net cash value equals cash value minus loans and interest plus bonus accumulations.

stem: What is the defining feature that distinguishes endowment insurance from whole life?

options.C: It pays nothing on death during the term
options.D: It has a fixed maturity date with a maturity value on survival
options.A: It carries the lowest premium of the three traditional products
options.B: It can only be written as non-participating

explanation: Endowment's defining feature is a fixed maturity date paying a maturity value on survival, or the death benefit if death occurs during the term. It has the highest premium of the three traditional products due to a heavy savings element, not the lowest.

stem: For an anticipated ('money-back') endowment that pays cash sums at intervals, how is the death benefit affected by cash payments already received?

options.A: The death benefit is NOT reduced by cash payments already received
options.B: The death benefit is paid only if no cash payments were taken
options.C: The death benefit is reduced by every cash payment already made
options.D: The policy pays only on survival and nothing on death

explanation: For an anticipated (money-back) endowment the death benefit is NOT reduced by the periodic cash payments already received. A pure endowment, by contrast, pays only on survival and nothing on death.

stem: Ranking Term, Whole Life and Endowment by premium from lowest to highest, the correct order is:

options.D: Endowment, Whole Life, Term
options.A: Term, Whole Life, Endowment
options.B: Whole Life, Term, Endowment
options.C: Term, Endowment, Whole Life

explanation: Premium ranking is Term lowest, Whole Life in the middle, Endowment highest, because endowment carries the heaviest savings element. The reverse order (Endowment, Whole Life, Term) is therefore incorrect.

stem: Which point-of-sale document is required only for Investment-Linked Policies and not for traditional life policies?

options.A: The Product Summary
options.B: The Product Highlights Sheet
options.C: The Policy Illustration
options.D: The Cover Page

explanation: Under MAS Notice FAA-N16 the Product Highlights Sheet is required for ILPs only. The Cover Page, Product Summary and Policy Illustration are given for life policies generally.

stem: Which statement best describes a rider (supplementary benefit)?

options.A: A supplementary benefit attached to a basic policy that adds cover for an extra premium
options.B: A standalone policy sold independently of any basic plan
options.C: A discount applied to the basic premium
options.D: A mandatory feature that comes free with every policy

explanation: A rider is a supplementary benefit attaching to a basic policy, adding cover the basic contract lacks, for an extra premium and shown in the schedule with an endorsement. It cannot exist as a standalone policy.

stem: Which statement about the general rules for riders is correct?

options.A: A rider can be bought without any basic policy
options.B: Riders have no cash value and terminate when the policy converts to Extended Term Insurance
options.C: A rider's term may exceed the basic policy's term
options.D: You may cancel the basic policy but keep the rider running

explanation: Riders carry no cash value and automatically terminate when the basic policy converts to ETI. You cannot buy a rider without a basic policy, nor keep a rider after cancelling the basic policy, and a rider's term cannot exceed the basic policy's.

stem: When is a Waiver of Premium on Critical Illness rider NOT worth recommending?

options.A: When the basic cover already gives 100% acceleration of the death benefit on CI
options.B: When the client is young and healthy
options.C: When the waiting period is only six months
options.D: When the policy is a regular-premium whole life plan

explanation: If the basic cover already accelerates 100% of the death benefit on CI, the policy pays out and terminates on a CI claim, so there are no future premiums left to waive. The WoP-on-CI rider would then be redundant.

stem: Once TPD instalment payments begin under a Total and Permanent Disability rider, what happens to the other riders on the policy?

options.A: The death benefit is doubled
options.B: All other riders terminate except an Extended TPD rider
options.C: Only the Critical Illness rider survives
options.D: All riders continue unaffected

explanation: Once TPD instalments begin, all other riders terminate except an Extended TPD rider. Aggregate TPD is typically capped around $2m per insurer, and nothing is paid for intentionally self-inflicted injury.

stem: How does an Acceleration (accelerator) Critical Illness rider differ from an Additional Benefit CI rider?

options.B: Acceleration pays on top of the basic sum assured, leaving death cover intact
options.C: Acceleration pre-pays part or all of the basic sum assured, so it reduces the basic cover
options.D: Both pay entirely separately from the basic sum assured
options.A: Additional Benefit reduces the basic sum assured while Acceleration adds to it

explanation: Acceleration pre-pays part or all of the BASIC sum assured, so it reduces the basic cover; 100% acceleration terminates the policy. Additional Benefit instead pays ON TOP of the basic sum assured, leaving death cover intact, so saying Additional Benefit reduces cover while Acceleration adds to it reverses the two.

stem: Regarding Critical Illness rider periods, which statement is correct?

options.A: There is no waiting period for CI riders in Singapore
options.B: A 90-day waiting period applies to all CI riders, while a 30-day survival period applies only to the Additional Benefit
options.C: A 30-day waiting period applies to all CI riders
options.D: A 90-day survival period applies to the Acceleration Benefit only

explanation: The 90-day waiting period (to defeat anti-selection) applies to all CI riders; the 30-day survival period applies only to the Additional Benefit. The 37 covered critical illnesses are standardised across insurers in Singapore.

stem: To which type of basic policy can a term rider be attached?

options.A: Any policy including another term policy
options.B: Only a permanent policy such as whole life
options.C: Only a term policy
options.D: Only a single-premium ILP

explanation: A term rider only attaches to a PERMANENT policy, never to a term policy; on a term policy you simply raise the term sum assured instead. It is sized as a ratio to the basic SA, e.g. 3:1 or 5:1.

stem: The Family Income Benefit rider on a juvenile policy is structured as which type of rider?

options.A: A whole life rider
options.B: An increasing term rider
options.C: A decreasing term rider
options.D: A level term rider

explanation: Family Income Benefit is a decreasing term rider paying a regular income to a child: the earlier the payor dies, the more total income the child receives, because more payments remain. Later death leaves fewer payments, hence decreasing.

stem: Under a Payor Benefit rider on a juvenile policy, what happens if the paying parent dies or becomes disabled before the child reaches the specified age?

options.A: The child must begin paying premiums immediately
options.B: The policy immediately pays out the full sum assured
options.C: The policy lapses with no value
options.D: Premiums are waived until the child reaches that specified age

explanation: If the payor dies or becomes disabled before the child reaches the specified age (e.g. 21 or 25), premiums are waived until the child reaches that age, keeping the policy in force. Some versions add CI to the triggering events.

stem: What does a Guaranteed Insurability Option (GIO) rider actually provide?

options.A: A right to buy additional insurance at set intervals or life events without evidence of insurability
options.B: Immediate additional life cover at no cost
options.C: A waiver of premiums on disability
options.D: A guaranteed investment return on the policy

explanation: GIO is not cover itself but a RIGHT to buy future additional insurance at set intervals or life events (e.g. ages 30/35/40, marriage, birth of a child) without evidence of insurability. Skipping one option date does not forfeit the next.

stem: An Accidental Death Benefit rider is often called 'double indemnity' because it:

options.A: Covers two lives under one rider
options.B: Pays twice the premium back on maturity
options.C: Doubles the cash value each year
options.D: Pays an additional amount, usually equal to the basic sum assured, on accidental death

explanation: ADB pays an additional amount, usually equal to the basic sum assured, on accidental death, hence 'double indemnity'. Sold standalone by a general insurer, it becomes a Personal Accident policy.

stem: Compared with the Accidental Death Benefit rider, the Accidental Death and Dismemberment (AD&D) rider additionally covers:

options.A: Loss of employment income
options.B: Dismemberment or functional permanent loss of limbs, sight, hearing or speech
options.C: Hospitalisation cash for any admission
options.D: Death from any cause including illness

explanation: AD&D is ADB plus cover for dismemberment (severance/amputation) or functional permanent loss of limbs, sight, hearing or speech, paid as a percentage of the rider SA. It suits blue-collar and higher-risk occupations.

stem: How does a Hospital Cash (Income) Benefit rider pay out?

options.A: It pays a fixed daily benefit for hospital confinement regardless of actual charges
options.B: It pays only if the stay exceeds 90 days
options.C: It reimburses the exact hospital bill incurred
options.D: It pays a lump sum equal to the sum assured on admission

explanation: Hospital Cash pays a fixed daily benefit (e.g. $150/day) for confinement regardless of actual charges, subject to limits and a waiting period. Because it pays from the first dollar it is useful to cover the co-payment or deductible under a separate Medical Expense policy.

stem: Which statement about a participating ('with-profits') policy is correct?

options.A: Participating policies never pay any bonuses
options.B: Each policy owner holds visible, identifiable units in the par fund
options.C: The guaranteed benefits need not be paid if the par fund underperforms
options.D: Par fund assets are pooled and not identifiable per policy owner, and guaranteed benefits must be paid regardless of fund performance

explanation: Par fund assets are pooled and NOT identifiable per policy owner, and the insurer must pay guaranteed benefits regardless of fund performance, injecting capital if needed. This contrasts with an ILP where each owner holds visible units.

stem: In a participating policy, which of the following is a NON-guaranteed benefit?

options.A: The guaranteed cash value
options.B: The bonuses
options.C: The face amount shown on page one
options.D: The sum assured

explanation: Non-guaranteed benefits are the bonuses, whose level depends on investment performance, expenses and claims. The sum assured and guaranteed cash values are guaranteed. Note that once a bonus is added it generally cannot be taken away.

stem: What is the purpose of 'smoothing' in a participating fund?

options.A: To eliminate all investment risk from the fund
options.B: To hold back bonuses in good years so they can be sustained in bad years
options.C: To guarantee a fixed bonus rate for the life of the policy
options.D: To make declared bonuses exactly track market movements each year

explanation: Smoothing means insurers hold back bonuses in good years to sustain them in bad years, so declared bonuses do not track market swings. It reduces volatility of declarations, it does not make them track the market or become fixed.

stem: How does a Compound Reversionary Bonus (CRB) differ from a Simple Reversionary Bonus (SRB)?

options.A: CRB is calculated on the sum assured plus bonuses already attached, giving increasing bonuses
options.B: CRB can be removed once declared
options.C: CRB is paid only at termination of the policy
options.D: CRB is calculated on the sum assured only, giving level bonuses

explanation: CRB is calculated on the sum assured PLUS bonuses already attached, so it compounds and gives increasing bonuses. SRB is calculated on the sum assured only, giving level bonuses. Once declared, either bonus is guaranteed.

stem: Which statement about the terminal bonus is correct?

options.A: It is added to the sum assured of an in-force policy each year
options.B: It is always a fixed dollar amount unrelated to performance
options.C: It is guaranteed from the first policy anniversary
options.D: It is credited only on termination and tends to fluctuate more than the reversionary bonus

explanation: Terminal bonus is added only on termination (maturity, death, TPD or surrender), usually after a minimum period in force, and fluctuates more than the reversionary bonus because it fine-tunes smoothing. It is never credited to a live in-force policy.

stem: An interim bonus is paid to a participating policy that:

options.A: Has been in force for over 25 years
options.B: Has never claimed any bonus before
options.C: Elects to receive cash dividends instead of bonuses
options.D: Terminates early in the year before the annual bonus declaration is finalised

explanation: An interim bonus is paid to policies terminating early in the year before the annual bonus declaration is finalised (declaration is typically March or April after audited accounts). Cash dividends are a separate alternative distribution method.

stem: Who analyses the participating fund each year and recommends both the bonus to allocate and the amount to reserve?

options.A: The external auditor
options.B: The Board of Directors alone
options.C: The Appointed Actuary, whose recommendation the Board approves
options.D: The Monetary Authority of Singapore

explanation: The Appointed Actuary analyses the fund and recommends the bonus and the reserve; the Board of Directors approves it. Guiding considerations include fairness between generations, solvency, and consistency with stable long-term returns.

stem: Under the 90/10 rule, how is the insurer's profit from the participating fund limited?

options.C: To 10% of the total value of the entire par fund
options.D: To one-ninth of the amount allocated to policy owners as bonus
options.A: To 90% of the distributable surplus
options.B: To a fixed annual dollar cap set by MAS

explanation: The insurer's profit is limited to one-ninth of the amount allocated to policy owners as bonus, i.e. 90% of distributable surplus to owners and 10% to the insurer. It is not 10% of the whole par fund computed separately, which is the trap.

stem: Under the Risk-Based Capital framework, which of the following must the actuary reserve for when valuing the policy liability?

options.A: Only the guaranteed benefits
options.B: Only future bonuses, since guaranteed benefits need no reserve
options.C: Guaranteed benefits, future non-guaranteed bonuses, and a Provision for Adverse Deviation
options.D: Only the Provision for Adverse Deviation

explanation: Under the RBC framework the actuary reserves for guaranteed benefits, future non-guaranteed bonuses, and a Provision for Adverse Deviation (PAD). Reserving only for guaranteed benefits would understate the liability.

stem: Regarding the Policy Illustration for a participating policy, which statement is correct?

options.A: Only the representative needs to sign the cover page
options.B: The higher projection rate is capped by LIA's maximum best-estimate long-term return and both parties sign every page
options.C: The projection uses a single guaranteed rate of return
options.D: 'Your Guide to Participating Policies' must always be handed over at point of sale

explanation: The Policy Illustration projects at two rates (e.g. 3.75% and 5.25%), the higher of which cannot exceed LIA's maximum best-estimate long-term return, and client and representative sign every page. 'Your Guide to Participating Policies' is generic and provided on request, not compulsory.

stem: Which statement about the Internal Governance Policy for a participating fund is correct?

options.D: It must be published to all consumers by law
options.A: It must be approved and reviewed annually by the board, and need not be disclosed to consumers
options.B: It is optional and many insurers do not maintain one
options.C: It is prepared by MAS on the insurer's behalf

explanation: Every insurer with a par fund must maintain an Internal Governance Policy approved and reviewed annually by the board; it need not be disclosed to consumers, though insurers may choose to. It is mandatory, so calling it optional is wrong.

stem: What is the single most important consequence of an Investment-Linked Policy for the policy owner?

options.A: It provides no guaranteed cash value, and the owner bears the investment risk
options.B: It pays annual reversionary bonuses
options.C: It cannot ever lapse regardless of fund performance
options.D: It guarantees a minimum surrender value

explanation: An ILP provides NO guaranteed cash value; its value rises and falls entirely with sub-fund performance and the owner bears the investment risk. It does not pay reversionary bonuses, which belong to participating traditional policies.

stem: ILPs can be classified by premium frequency. A single-premium plan built up over time through repeated top-ups is often described as a:

options.A: Recurring single premium ILP
options.B: Limited payment ILP
options.C: Yearly renewable ILP
options.D: Regular premium ILP

explanation: Single-premium ILPs are savings-focused, and repeated top-ups form a 'recurring single premium'. Regular-premium ILPs are usually for protection with variable cover, which is a different classification.

stem: Under an ILP, what does a 'premium holiday' feature allow?

options.A: The policy is converted into a traditional whole life plan
options.B: The insurer refunds all premiums for a year
options.C: The owner doubles the sum assured for free
options.D: The owner stops paying premiums while the insurer sells units to cover charges

explanation: A premium holiday lets the owner stop paying while the insurer sells units to cover ongoing charges, provided the value is sufficient. It is not a refund of premiums, and it does not convert the policy.

stem: Why is a regular-premium ILP generally unsuitable for an older client whose main aim is investment?

options.A: Heavy early-year charges combined with a short horizon and inability to sustain premiums cripple returns
options.B: ILPs guarantee returns only for those under 40
options.C: The sub-funds are unavailable to older investors
options.D: Older clients cannot legally buy ILPs

explanation: Regular-premium ILPs carry heavy early-year charges, so a long horizon matters; for older clients the deciding issue is usually the ability to sustain premiums into retirement. High initial costs plus a short horizon cripple returns.

stem: Under the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS), which type of ILP may a member newly fund with CPF savings?

options.A: Yearly renewable term ILPs only
options.B: Any ILP regardless of premium type
options.C: Regular-premium ILPs only
options.D: Single-premium ILPs only

explanation: Under CPFIS only single-premium ILPs are allowed. Members who bought regular-premium plans before 2001 may continue paying with CPF, but those are grandfathered, not newly permitted.

stem: Which is a key difference between an ILP and a traditional participating policy?

options.A: An ILP guarantees no minimum surrender value, while a participating policy guarantees a minimum
options.B: Participating sub-funds publish daily unit prices while ILPs do not
options.C: A participating policy guarantees no minimum surrender value, while an ILP does
options.D: ILP charges are bundled while participating premiums are unbundled

explanation: An ILP guarantees no minimum surrender value, whereas a participating policy guarantees a minimum. ILP charges are unbundled and transparent while par premiums are bundled, and it is the ILP sub-fund that publishes daily unit prices, so the reversed statements are wrong.

stem: Under a bid-offer (dual) pricing model, at which prices does the policy owner buy and sell units?

options.A: Buy at bid, sell at offer
options.B: Buy at offer, sell at bid
options.C: Buy at bid, sell at bid
options.D: Buy and sell at the same single price

explanation: Under bid-offer (dual) pricing you buy at offer and sell at bid, with a spread of about 5% acting as the initial sales charge (remember BOSB: Buy at Offer, Sell at Bid). Single pricing uses one price with the sales charge disclosed separately.

stem: Under a front-end loaded regular-premium ILP, how does the premium allocation rate typically behave?

options.A: It starts at 100% and falls over time
options.B: It allocates less than 100% in early years, rising to 100% later
options.C: It is fixed at 50% throughout the policy
options.D: It allocates 100% from the start but charges a fee on early surrender

explanation: Front-end loading allocates less than 100% in the early years, rising to 100% (sometimes above) later. Allocating 100% from the start but charging a fee on early surrender describes back-end loading instead.

stem: Under forward pricing for an ILP, orders to buy or sell units are settled at:

options.A: A price fixed at the start of each month
options.B: The last published price before the order
options.C: An average of the day's high and low prices
options.D: The next computed price after the order

explanation: With forward pricing the manager recomputes the NAV after market close, and orders settle at the next computed price: buying at the next offer, selling at the next bid. It is not the last-published or a fixed price.

stem: When ILP charges are met by selling units, at which price are the charges converted into units to be cancelled?

options.A: The average of bid and offer
options.B: The bid price
options.C: The offer price
options.D: The original issue price

explanation: Charges met by selling units are converted at the BID price, so the spread bites. The first sub-fund switch each year is usually free, and the sub-fund management fee runs 0.5% to 2% p.a., but the conversion price for charges is the bid.

stem: In a regular-premium ILP the premium can stay level even though the cost of insurance rises with age. What risk does this create if the sub-fund performs poorly?

options.A: The units may become inadequate to meet rising insurance charges, forcing a top-up or reduced cover
options.B: The sum assured automatically increases each year
options.C: The insurer must refund all past charges
options.D: The bid-offer spread is waived permanently

explanation: The level premium works because units are sold each month to pay the rising insurance charge; if the fund performs poorly the units may become inadequate, forcing the owner to raise premiums or cut cover. Higher chosen protection consumes more units, leaving fewer to build value.

stem: For a regular-premium ILP, when may an insurer revise the scale of insurance coverage charges?

options.B: On any single policy at the insurer's discretion at any time
options.C: Only across an entire class of policies and only on a general, sustained worsening of claims experience
options.D: Never, since the charges are always guaranteed
options.A: Only when the stock market falls

explanation: The insurance charge scale can be revised, but only across an entire class of policies and only on a general and sustained worsening of claims experience, never in isolation on a single policy. The charges are not guaranteed, so 'never revised' is wrong.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an ILP from a unit trust?

options.A: Both fall under the Code on Collective Investment Schemes
options.B: An ILP provides insurance cover plus investment and has a 14-day free-look, while a unit trust is investment only with a 7-day cancellation period
options.C: A unit trust provides a death benefit while an ILP does not
options.D: An ILP has a 7-day free-look while a unit trust has 14 days

explanation: An ILP provides insurance cover (a death benefit) plus investment and has a 14-day free-look; a unit trust is investment only with a 7-day cancellation period. ILPs fall under the Insurance Act and MAS Notice 307, unit trusts under the Code on CIS and the SFA.

stem: What is the key difference between an accumulation and a distribution sub-fund structure?

options.A: Accumulation pays income out to owners; distribution reinvests it
options.B: Accumulation has a fixed unit price while distribution's price floats
options.C: Accumulation reinvests income back into the fund; distribution pays income out to owners
options.D: Both pay income out but at different times

explanation: Accumulation ploughs investment income back into the fund, enhancing unit prices; distribution pays income out to owners as additional units or dividends. The unit price still moves with capital gains and losses in both.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between fund types?

options.A: A feeder fund feeds directly into the mother fund and experiences the same price fluctuations
options.B: A mirror fund feeds directly into a mother fund and shares its price movements
options.C: A mother fund is a preset mix of funds matched to a risk profile
options.D: A portfolio duplicates the composition of a single existing fund

explanation: A feeder fund feeds directly into the mother fund and shares its price fluctuations. A mirror fund merely copies an existing fund's composition, and a portfolio is a preset mix of funds matched to a risk profile, so the other statements misattribute these definitions.

stem: Which type of sub-fund is generally lowest risk with a short recommended horizon and capital unlikely to fall?

options.A: Cash / money-market sub-fund
options.B: Geographically specialised sub-fund
options.C: Property sub-fund
options.D: Equity sub-fund

explanation: A cash / money-market sub-fund is low risk with a horizon up to about 3 years and capital unlikely to fall. Equity and geographically specialised funds are higher risk with roughly 10-year horizons.

stem: Because property is illiquid, a property fund may defer unit redemptions for up to 12 months, EXCEPT in the case of:

options.A: A switch to another fund
options.B: A premium holiday request
options.C: A partial withdrawal
options.D: A death claim

explanation: Property fund redemptions can be deferred for up to 12 months due to illiquidity, but never on a death claim. Death is the exception where redemption cannot be deferred.

stem: How does a capital-guaranteed fund typically try to preserve capital while offering some growth?

options.A: By holding only cash and money-market instruments
options.B: By investing entirely in property
options.C: By holding mostly equities with a small bond allocation
options.D: By putting most money in bonds to preserve capital and the balance in derivatives for growth

explanation: Capital-guaranteed funds put most money in bonds to preserve capital and the balance in derivatives (usually options) for upside. They are commonly closed-end with a fixed maturity, tenure around 4-7 years.

stem: What distinguishes a managed (balanced) fund from a managed portfolio?

options.A: Both pick individual assets but with different managers
options.B: A managed fund picks which funds to invest in; a managed portfolio picks assets
options.C: A managed portfolio is always single-manager while a managed fund is multi-manager
options.D: A managed fund picks which assets to buy; a managed portfolio picks which funds to invest in

explanation: A managed (balanced) fund is one fund whose manager chooses which assets to buy; a managed portfolio (risk-rated/lifestyle fund) is multiple funds whose manager chooses which funds to invest in. Managed fund picks assets, managed portfolio picks funds.

stem: As an education or retirement target date approaches, how is the switching facility typically used?

options.A: Stop switching altogether to lock in current prices
options.B: Switch from cash into volatile equity funds to chase returns
options.C: Switch from volatile equity funds into more stable cash or fixed-income funds
options.D: Switch entirely into property funds for the final year

explanation: As the target date nears, the owner switches from volatile equity funds into more stable cash or fixed-income funds to protect accumulated value. Moving into more volatile equities near the target would raise the risk of a shortfall.

stem: An adviser persuades a client to surrender one ILP and buy another with no real benefit, purely to earn fresh commission. This is best described as:

options.A: Improper product switching (churning), which is prohibited misconduct
options.B: A permitted automatic sub-fund switch
options.C: Dollar cost averaging
options.D: Legitimate fund switching within an ILP

explanation: Getting a client to surrender one product and buy another with no real benefit, purely to churn commissions, is improper product switching and prohibited misconduct. Legitimate fund switching simply moves money between sub-funds within the same ILP.

stem: Which type of interest does the M9 syllabus use throughout its computations, and why does it matter?

options.A: Compound interest, because interest is earned on principal plus accumulated interest
options.B: Nominal interest with no compounding at all
options.C: A blend of simple and compound interest depending on the product
options.D: Simple interest, because it applies the rate to the original principal only

explanation: M9 uses compound interest throughout: interest is earned on principal plus previously accumulated interest, giving a higher balance over time than simple interest, which applies the rate to the original principal only.

stem: Using PV = FV / (1 + i)^n, what happens to the present value as the interest rate i or the number of periods n rises?

options.A: The present value falls
options.B: The present value stays the same
options.C: The present value first rises then falls
options.D: The present value rises

explanation: In discounting, PV falls as i or n rises, because a higher rate or longer time means you need less money today to reach the same future value. In compounding, by contrast, FV rises with i and n.

stem: A rate of 10% per annum is quoted nominal but compounded semi-annually. Which statement is correct?

options.C: The effective rate equals the nominal rate at 10%
options.D: The effective rate is 10.25%, higher than the nominal rate
options.A: The effective rate is 9.75%, lower than the nominal rate
options.B: The effective and nominal rates are equal only when compounding is monthly

explanation: 10% nominal compounded semi-annually gives an effective rate of 10.25% ((1.05 x 1.05) - 1). The effective rate is always higher than the nominal rate, and the two are equal only under annual compounding, so 'effective equals nominal at 10%' is the trap.

stem: When a question asks for the offer price at the 'beginning of Year 4', how many compounding periods should you apply to the current offer price?

options.A: 4 periods
options.B: 5 periods
options.C: 3 periods
options.D: 2 periods

explanation: 'Beginning of Year 4' means the end of Year 3, which is 3 compounding periods, not 4. Miscounting the periods is the classic error in these questions.

stem: Where u is the value of units at bid price and v is the sum assured, which pairing of death benefit methods is correct?

options.A: DB3 = u only; DB4 = v only
options.B: DB3 = higher of u or v; DB4 = u + v
options.C: DB3 = v only; DB4 = u + v
options.D: DB3 = u + v; DB4 = higher of u or v

explanation: DB3 = units + sum assured (u + v); DB4 = the higher of units or sum assured. Do not swap these two, which is the common error. DB1 is units only and DB2 is sum assured only.

stem: For the same sum assured, how does the death benefit and mortality charge under DB3 compare with DB4?

options.A: DB3 and DB4 always pay exactly the same benefit
options.B: DB3 pays less and costs less in mortality charges
options.C: DB4 always pays more than DB3
options.D: DB3 pays more and therefore costs more in mortality charges

explanation: DB3 (u + v) always pays a higher death benefit than DB4 (higher of u or v) for the same sum assured, and a higher death benefit means a higher mortality charge. So DB3 always costs more in mortality charges.

stem: How is the monthly mortality charge determined under DB4 (higher of u or v) when the value of units u is less than the sum assured v?

options.D: (q/12) x v, the full sum assured
options.A: (q/12) x (v - u), the excess of sum assured over units
options.B: (q/12) x u, the value of the units
options.C: Zero, because units always cover the sum assured

explanation: Under DB4 the units offset the sum assured, so the mortality charge is (q/12) x (v - u), or zero if u is at least v. Under DB3 the units offset nothing and the charge would be (q/12) x v on the full sum assured.

stem: For a single premium or a top-up into an ILP, what allocation rate is usually applied to purchase units?

options.D: It varies each year under a front-end loading scale

explanation: Single premiums and top-ups usually allocate 100% to purchase units. The rising scale (e.g. Year 1 15%, Year 2 30%) applies to regular premiums under front-end loading, not to single premiums or top-ups.

stem: When charges are deducted AFTER units have been allocated, at which price are the charges converted into units to be cancelled?

options.A: The offer price
options.B: The mid price between bid and offer
options.C: The bid price
options.D: The original allocation price

explanation: Charges deducted after allocation are always converted to units at the BID price, so the bid-offer spread bites and fewer units remain. Converting at the offer price would understate the units cancelled.

stem: At which price are units valued when a policy owner makes a partial withdrawal or a full surrender of an ILP?

options.A: The offer price for withdrawal and bid price for surrender
options.B: The bid price for withdrawal and offer price for surrender
options.C: The offer price for both
options.D: The bid price for both

explanation: You always cash out at the BID price, whether making a partial withdrawal or a full surrender. For a withdrawal, units cancelled = withdrawal amount / bid price; for surrender, value = units x bid price less any surrender charges.

stem: The 'return on gross premium' on a single-premium ILP is best described as:

options.A: The total dollar profit minus all fees
options.B: The bid-offer spread charged at outset
options.C: The simple interest earned on the premium each year
options.D: The compound rate that turns the single premium into the eventual surrender value

explanation: Return on gross premium is the compound rate that grows the single premium into the eventual surrender value; you set Premium x (1 + i)^n = cash value, solve for the factor, then match it to the closest FVIF. It is a compound growth rate, not simple interest.

stem: At the age of 10, a mortality table shows 98,509 lives are living at the start of the year and 119 of them will die during the year. If each death claim is S$10,000, what pure death-protection premium must each living person pay for the year (ignoring expenses and investment income)?
explanation: Total claims = 119 x S$10,000 = S$1,190,000. Spread across the 98,509 living: S$1,190,000 / 98,509 = S$12.08 per person. The value S$1.19 wrongly divides the S$10,000 claim by the number of deaths incorrectly instead of computing the pooled cost per living member.

stem: An ILP account holds 5,000 units, the bid price is S$3.04, and the sum assured is 150% of the S$10,000 single premium. Using the DB3 method (units plus sum assured), what is the death benefit?
explanation: Value of units u = 5,000 x S$3.04 = S$15,200. Sum assured v = 150% x S$10,000 = S$15,000. DB3 = u + v = S$15,200 + S$15,000 = S$30,200. The tempting S$15,200 is the DB4 answer (higher of u or v), not DB3.

stem: Using the same figures (5,000 units at bid price S$3.04, sum assured S$15,000), what is the death benefit under the DB4 method (higher of units or sum assured)?
explanation: Value of units u = 5,000 x S$3.04 = S$15,200; sum assured v = S$15,000. DB4 = higher of u or v = S$15,200. The value S$30,200 is DB3 (u + v), while S$15,000 wrongly picks the lower of the two instead of the higher.

stem: The offer price of an ILP sub-fund in Year 1 is S$1.49 and it grows at 4% per annum. What is the offer price at the beginning of Year 3?
explanation: Beginning of Year 3 means the end of Year 2, so 2 compounding periods: S$1.49 x 1.04^2 = S$1.49 x 1.0816 = S$1.61. Applying only 1 period gives S$1.55, and 3 periods gives S$1.68.

stem: A single premium of S$10,000 buys units at an offer price of S$1.50. Total fees and charges are S$400 (a S$150 policy fee plus a S$250 admin and mortality charge), deducted after allocation with a 5% bid-offer spread. How many units remain after charges?
explanation: Units purchased = S$10,000 / S$1.50 = 6,666.67. Bid price = 0.95 x S$1.50 = S$1.43. Units cancelled for charges = S$400 / S$1.43 = 279.72. Remaining = 6,666.67 - 279.72 = 6,386.95. The value 6,400.00 wrongly converts the charges at the offer price (S$400/1.50 = 266.67) instead of the bid price.

stem: An ILP uses the DB3 method with a sum assured of S$100,000. The annual cost of life cover is S$1.50 per S$1,000. What is the monthly mortality charge?
explanation: Under DB3 the charge is (q/12) x v = (S$1.50 / 1,000 / 12) x S$100,000 = S$150 / 12 = S$12.50 per month. The S$150.00 figure is the full annual charge without dividing by 12.

stem: An ILP uses the DB4 method with a sum assured of S$100,000 and units currently worth S$581.40. The annual cost of life cover is S$1.50 per S$1,000. What is the monthly mortality charge?
explanation: Under DB4 the charge is (q/12) x (v - u) = (S$1.50 / 1,000 / 12) x (S$100,000 - S$581.40) = 0.000125 x S$99,418.60 = S$12.43. The value S$12.50 is the DB3 charge on the full S$100,000, ignoring the unit offset.

stem: A policy owner makes a partial withdrawal of S$3,000 from an ILP when the bid price is S$2.00. How many units are cancelled?

options.A: 3,000 units
options.B: 1,500 units
options.C: 1,429 units
options.D: 6,000 units

explanation: Units cancelled = withdrawal amount / bid price = S$3,000 / S$2.00 = 1,500 units. Using an offer price of S$2.10 (a 5% spread) instead of the bid price would wrongly give about 1,429 units.

stem: An ILP holds 9,015.77 units. At surrender the applicable bid price is S$2.20 and there are no surrender charges. What is the surrender value?
explanation: Surrender value = number of units x current bid price = 9,015.77 x S$2.20 = S$19,834.69. Valuing the units at S$2.00 instead of the S$2.20 bid price would wrongly give S$18,031.54.

stem: A single premium of S$10,000 grows to a surrender value of S$17,947.33 after 10 years. Using the FVIF table (the closest factor to 1.7947 at n=10 is 1.7908), what is the approximate return on gross premium?

options.A: 10% per annum
options.B: 8% per annum
options.C: 6% per annum
options.D: 5% per annum

explanation: S$10,000 x (1 + i)^10 = S$17,947.33, so (1 + i)^10 = 1.7947. At n=10 the closest FVIF is 1.7908, which corresponds to 6% per annum. It is a compound growth rate, not the simple average of about 8% per year.

stem: S$5,000 is deposited today at 9% compound annual interest. Using FV = PV x (1 + i)^n, what is the future value at the end of Year 7 (1.09^7 = 1.828039)?
explanation: FV = S$5,000 x 1.09^7 = S$5,000 x 1.828039 = S$9,140.20. The value S$8,150 mistakenly applies simple interest (S$5,000 x (1 + 0.09 x 7)); S$9,743.59 is the result at 10% instead of 9%.

stem: You will need S$100,000 in four years for a house down-payment and can earn 4% compound interest. Using PV = FV / (1 + i)^n (1.04^4 = 1.16986), how much should you set aside today?
explanation: PV = S$100,000 / 1.04^4 = S$100,000 / 1.16986 = S$85,477.39. The value S$82,270.67 discounts at 5% instead of 4%, and S$88,896.79 discounts over 3 years instead of 4.

stem: Following a single-premium ILP, a top-up of S$5,000 is made in the third year. The initial offer price was S$1.50 growing at 7% p.a. (1.07^3 = 1.2250), a 5% bid-offer spread applies, the top-up fee is S$80 and the admin-with-mortality charge is 1.5% of the top-up. How many net units does the top-up add?
explanation: Offer price = S$1.50 x 1.07^3 = S$1.84; bid = 0.95 x S$1.84 = S$1.75. Units purchased = S$5,000 / S$1.84 = 2,717.39. Charges = S$80 + (1.5% x S$5,000 = S$75) = S$155; units cancelled = S$155 / S$1.75 = 88.57. Net = 2,717.39 - 88.57 = 2,628.82. The figure 2,717.39 omits the charge deduction entirely.

stem: A client worries about outliving his retirement savings. Which product is specifically designed to address this concern?

options.A: An annuity, because it provides guaranteed income for as long as the annuitant lives
options.B: A term life insurance policy, because it pays a lump sum on death
options.C: A whole life policy, because it builds cash value over time
options.D: A personal accident policy, because it covers disability

explanation: An annuity protects against living too long (longevity risk) by paying income for life; it is the mirror image of life insurance, which protects against dying too soon. Term life pays only on death and does nothing for someone who outlives their savings.

stem: Under CPF LIFE, which statement about the payout plans and deferment is correct?

options.A: The Basic plan is the default and gives the highest payouts
options.B: The Escalating plan starts lower and rises about 2% each year
options.C: Deferring the payout age reduces future payouts by about 7% per year
options.D: Members must start payouts at age 62

explanation: The Escalating plan begins with a lower payout that rises roughly 2% yearly. The Standard plan (not Basic) is the default with higher payouts, and deferring the payout age raises payouts by about 7% per year, not reduces them.

stem: In an annuity, the period running from the first premium until income payments begin is known as the:

options.A: Payout period
options.B: Grace period
options.C: Accumulation period
options.D: Vesting period

explanation: The accumulation period runs from the first premium until payouts start, while the insurer invests the premiums. The payout period is the later phase during which income is actually paid.

stem: A client wants an annuity whose payouts begin one payment period after purchase. Which statement about this annuity is true?

options.A: It can be funded by regular premiums spread over several years
options.B: It can only be bought using CPF Minimum Sum monies
options.C: Death before payouts begin forfeits the entire purchase price
options.D: It must be purchased with a single lump-sum premium

explanation: An immediate annuity pays out one period after purchase and can only be bought with a single lump-sum premium. Before payouts begin, death usually refunds the purchase price rather than forfeiting it.

stem: CPF Minimum Sum monies can be used to purchase which kind of annuity?

options.A: A deferred annuity only
options.B: An immediate annuity only
options.C: Either an immediate or a deferred annuity
options.D: A fixed-amount temporary annuity only

explanation: CPF Minimum Sum monies can only fund a deferred annuity, not an immediate one. Deferred annuities can also be bought with single or regular premiums, but the CPF restriction is the key distinction here.

stem: An annuitant is concerned that if he dies soon after payouts begin, his estate loses out. Which option leaves the estate nothing after his death?

options.A: Life Annuity with Period Certain
options.B: Pure Life (straight life) Annuity
options.C: Life Income with Refund
options.D: Joint and survivor annuity

explanation: A pure life annuity stops at death with nothing paid afterwards, so early death means receiving far less than the purchase price. The guaranteed-minimum versions pay less income but protect the estate through a period certain or a refund.

stem: A Fixed Amount annuity pays income until:

options.A: A specified number of years has elapsed, or death, whichever is first
options.B: The annuitant reaches age 85
options.C: The total payments reach a specified maximum, or death, whichever is first
options.D: The insurer declares that bonuses have been exhausted

explanation: A Fixed Amount annuity pays until the total reaches a specified maximum or the annuitant dies, whichever comes first. Paying until a specified period ends describes a Fixed Period annuity instead.

stem: Under a joint and survivor annuity, what typically happens after the first annuitant dies?

options.A: All payments stop immediately
options.B: The full purchase price is refunded to the estate
options.C: The surviving annuitant must buy a new policy
options.D: Payments continue, though the benefit may drop to a reduced percentage such as 50%

explanation: A joint and survivor annuity pays until all annuitants die, though the benefit may reduce (for example to 50%) after the first death. Payments stopping when one annuitant dies describes a joint life annuity, not a joint and survivor one.

stem: Annuity payouts are generally free from income tax EXCEPT when the annuity is:

options.A: From a partnership, the SRS, or an employer annuity replacing a pension
options.B: Bought with cash by a self-employed person
options.C: A single-life participating annuity
options.D: Purchased before the annuitant reaches age 55

explanation: Annuity payouts are tax-free except those from a partnership, the SRS, or an employer-bought annuity replacing a pension or employment benefit. A privately bought cash annuity by a self-employed person is not one of these exceptions.

stem: Why is the proposal form so important in a life insurance contract?

options.A: It is only a marketing document and not legally binding
options.B: It is the primary source of risk information and forms the basis of the contract
options.C: It replaces the need for a medical examination in all cases
options.D: It becomes valid only after the free-look period expires

explanation: The proposal form is the primary source of risk information, is incorporated into the policy, and forms the basis of the contract and any claim, so it must be completed truthfully under utmost good faith. It is far more than a marketing document.

stem: A client asks the adviser to sign the proposal form for her because she is busy. What is the correct position?

options.A: The adviser may sign if the client verbally agrees
options.B: The adviser may sign as long as the client countersigns later
options.C: The adviser must never sign the proposal form for the client
options.D: The adviser may sign only for third-party policies

explanation: The adviser must never sign the proposal form on behalf of the proposer, and the client must countersign any change. Non-disclosure would let the insurer void the policy from inception with nothing payable.

stem: Which statement about backdating a life policy is correct?

options.A: It raises the premium and can extend up to 12 months
options.B: It is freely available on all policy types including ILPs
options.C: It has no effect on premium and is used only for record-keeping
options.D: It lowers the premium, is capped at 6 months, and is not allowed on ILPs

explanation: Backdating to just before the last birthday secures a lower premium (charged on a next-birthday basis), is capped at 6 months, and is not available for some policies such as ILPs. It lowers rather than raises the premium.

stem: The section of a proposal form headed 'particulars of the proposer' is completed only when:

options.A: The policy is a third-party policy where insurable interest must be confirmed
options.B: The proposer is also the life insured
options.C: The policy is an investment-linked plan
options.D: The premium is paid by CPF

explanation: Particulars of the proposer are completed only for third-party policies, where the relationship confirms insurable interest. Where the proposer is also the life insured this separate confirmation is unnecessary.

stem: During the 14-day free-look period, if the client cancels a standard policy, what refund applies, and what restriction applies to undischarged bankrupts?

options.A: Full premium refund; bankrupts may buy freely
options.B: Premium refund less the risk-assessment cost; bankrupts need the Official Assignee's consent to buy new policies
options.C: No refund at all; bankrupts are barred entirely from insurance
options.D: Half the premium refunded; bankrupts need court approval

explanation: Free-look cancellation refunds the premium less the risk-assessment cost (or a full refund if the insurer rejects the proposal), and undischarged bankrupts cannot buy new policies without the Official Assignee's consent. A full refund applies only where the insurer itself rejects the proposal.

stem: In underwriting, which factor is the key indicator of moral hazard and guards against over-insurance?

options.A: Age, described as the point of departure
options.B: Occupation and physical condition
options.C: Financial condition, ensuring the sum assured bears a reasonable relationship to income
options.D: Medical history and family history

explanation: Financial condition is the main moral-hazard check, ensuring the sum assured is justified by income and preventing over-insurance. Age is the point of departure from the mortality table but is a physical, not a moral, hazard indicator.

stem: At what point does a compulsory HIV antibody test and the Lifestyle questionnaire generally kick in?

options.A: For every proposal regardless of sum assured
options.B: Only when the applicant is over age 60
options.C: Only when premiums are paid by CPF
options.D: When the sum assured exceeds $1 million, or for certain occupations

explanation: The HIV test and Lifestyle questionnaire apply above a $1m sum assured (all ages) or for certain occupations, the latter used solely to assess AIDS risk. They are not required on every proposal.

stem: An insurer decides to accept a higher-than-standard risk. Which set correctly lists the four ways it may do so?

options.A: Lien, change of plan, exclusion, or extra premium
options.B: Backdating, reinstatement, surrender, or assignment
options.C: Free-look, grace period, non-forfeiture, or lapse
options.D: Decline, postpone, refer, or counter-offer

explanation: The four ways to accept a higher risk are a lien, a change of plan, an exclusion, or extra premiums. Decline and postpone describe treatment of an uninsurable risk, not acceptance of a higher risk.

stem: On standard terms where the first premium did NOT accompany the application, when does cover commence?

options.A: Immediately when the application is signed
options.B: On receipt of the first premium within the set window after the letter of acceptance
options.C: Only after the free-look period ends
options.D: On the policy's first anniversary

explanation: On standard terms the insurer sends a letter of acceptance and cover starts on receipt of the first premium within a set window. Cover starting immediately on acceptance applies only where the premium accompanied the application.

stem: For a contributory group life plan, roughly what minimum participation level is required to control anti-selection?

options.A: About 25-40% of eligible members
options.B: About 50% of eligible members
options.C: About 70-90% of eligible members
options.D: 100% of eligible members without exception

explanation: Contributory group plans need about 70-90% participation to guard against anti-selection. Lower thresholds would allow healthier members to opt out, defeating the pooling that group underwriting relies on.

stem: Which statement about paying premiums via CPFIS or SRS is correct?

options.A: Both can pay regular monthly premiums like GIRO
options.B: Only SRS can fund an ILP; CPFIS cannot
options.C: Neither can be used for endowment policies
options.D: Both can only pay single or recurrent single premiums

explanation: CPFIS and SRS can only pay single or recurrent single premiums, not regular premiums. CPFIS can in fact fund endowment, annuity and ILP policies, so the restriction is on the premium mode, not the product.

stem: The Conditional Premium Deposit Receipt issued at the close of sale provides interim cover for:

options.A: Accidental death only, subject to a cap, pending official acceptance
options.B: Death from any cause, up to the full sum applied for
options.C: Critical illness only, for up to 90 days
options.D: Hospitalisation expenses only

explanation: The conditional receipt binds the insurer to conditional cover for accidental death only, typically within about 90 days and capped (often under $500,000 or the sum applied for, whichever is lower), pending acceptance. It does not cover death from any cause.

stem: Increasing the sum assured on an existing policy is generally allowed only for which type of policy?

options.A: Term life policies
options.B: Investment-linked policies (ILPs)
options.C: Whole life policies
options.D: Endowment policies

explanation: Increasing the sum assured is generally not allowed except for ILPs; non-ILPs usually permit it only in the first year with a health declaration. Insurers otherwise refuse alterations that increase their liability.

stem: A policyholder loses the physical policy document. What is the effect on the contract?

options.A: The contract is void and cover ends immediately
options.B: The insurer may cancel the policy without refund
options.C: The contract still exists; the document is only evidence, so claims are usually still paid with a letter of indemnity
options.D: The policyholder must reapply as a new customer

explanation: The policy document is only evidence of the contract, which exists independently, so insurers will usually still pay a claim with a letter of indemnity. Losing the paper does not void cover.

stem: Under section 4(8) of the Civil Law Act, a valid absolute assignment of a life policy requires that it be:

options.A: Made orally before two witnesses
options.B: Registered with MAS within 30 days
options.C: Approved by the Official Assignee
options.D: Absolute, in writing, and with written notice served on the insurer

explanation: An absolute assignment must be absolute, in writing, and accompanied by written notice served on the insurer. All three elements are required; oral assignment or MAS registration is not.

stem: What happens when the outstanding policy loan plus accrued interest exceeds the cash value of the policy?

options.A: The insurer terminates the policy with no premium refund
options.B: The insurer writes off the excess loan
options.C: The insurer increases the sum assured to cover it
options.D: The interest rate is automatically reduced

explanation: If loan plus accrued interest exceeds the cash value, the insurer terminates the policy with no premium refund. Interest typically accrues daily and compounds each anniversary, so unpaid balances can erode the cash value quickly.

stem: A policy is switched by a competing adviser from another company through misrepresentation. This practice is known as:

options.A: Churning
options.B: Twisting
options.C: Lapsing
options.D: Reinstatement

explanation: Twisting is improper replacement by a competing adviser; churning is done by the client's own errant adviser. Both are causes of lapsing but are distinguished by who is responsible.

stem: What is the MOST important condition an insurer requires before reinstating a lapsed policy?

options.A: Payment of a small administrative fee only
options.B: A fresh 14-day free-look period
options.C: Evidence of continued insurability
options.D: Consent of the original beneficiary

explanation: Evidence of continued insurability is the key reinstatement condition because it prevents anti-selection. The owner must also pay all arrears plus interest, and the incontestability and suicide clauses restart.

stem: An insurer must pay a surrender value once the policy has cash value and has been in force for at least:

options.A: 1 year
options.B: 2 years
options.C: 5 years
options.D: 3 years

explanation: Surrender value is payable for policies with cash value that have been in force at least 3 years. Note too that a bankrupt cannot surrender, since the interest vests in the Official Assignee.

stem: The core principle underlying all life insurance claims rules is that the insurer must:

options.A: Pay the right person the right amount, promptly
options.B: Minimise the amount paid on every claim
options.C: Delay payment until all beneficiaries agree
options.D: Pay only after a court order in every case

explanation: The core idea of claims is that the insurer must pay the right person the right amount, promptly; every claims rule is machinery for establishing entitlement. Minimising payment is not the governing principle.

stem: Which of the following would generally be treated as a proper claimant?

options.A: A creditor of the deceased with no assignment
